amend

uh-MEND — contains 'mend,' as in fixing something; to amend is to mend a flaw in a rule or plan. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To amend is to make a rule, law, or text better by changing or correcting part of it.

Lawmakers voted to amend the outdated regulation after years of complaints from small business owners.

Example

A club's rulebook bans anyone under sixteen from voting, even though many younger members have been active for years. After a long discussion, the members agree to amend that one rule so any member who has attended ten meetings can vote, regardless of age.

They are changing the rule to fix a flaw and make it work better. Unlike 'abolish,' which means to get rid of something completely, amend means to improve or revise part of it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

revise: To revise is to work back through a whole text, changing, cutting, and adding until it reads better overall. Amend is narrower: you amend a law or document by fixing one flawed part, while a revision can rework the entire draft.

reform: To reform is to improve a whole system — a school, a prison, a tax code — by changing how it operates. You amend a text or a law's wording; you reform the larger institution the law belongs to.

correct: To correct is simply to fix a mistake — a wrong date, a misspelled name. Amend goes further: when lawmakers amend a rule, they formally change its wording so the rule itself works better, not just fix a slip.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

worsen: to make something more bad or severe

preserve: to keep something exactly as it is

Where it sits · how deep the fix goes — adjust → amend → overhaul

adjust vs. amend: Adjust is weaker than amend — adjusting something is a small tweak, while amending it usually means a more formal, deliberate correction to fix a real flaw.

overhaul vs. amend: Overhaul is stronger than amend: amending a policy fixes one flawed part, but overhauling it means rebuilding the entire thing from the ground up.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — a- (ad-)

prefix — a- (ad-): to (Latin)

root — -mend-

root — -mend-: fault, flaw, blemish (Latin (menda))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin emendare combined e- (out) with menda ('a fault') to mean 'to remove a fault.' To amend something is, at its root, to correct a flaw in it.

Use the root in a new word: mend

Use the root in a new word: mend: He spent most of Saturday out in the yard, mending the old gate.
